item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Amid genocide in Gaza, why must Palestinian journalists uphold the illusion of neutrality?
item.description:
Amid genocide in Gaza, why must Palestinian journalists uphold the illusion of neutrality?

Submitted by Ahmed Abu Artema on Wed, 08/19/2026 - 08:48
Israel has killed over 200 media workers to eliminate witnesses to war crimes, but people enduring the onslaught are the best equipped to document the violence
Mourners gather around the body of Al Jazeera Mubasher cameraman Ahmed Wishah, his press vest laid on the shroud, at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, on 21 June 2026 (Reuters/Mahmoud Issa)
Off

On 20 June 2026, the Israeli army killed Al Jazeera Mubasher cameraman Ahmed Wishah in a drone strike, less than two and a half months after the killing of his brother, Al Jazeera Mubasher correspondent Mohammed Wishah, who was targeted by the same army on 8 April.

After Mohammed's death, Ahmed appeared on Al Jazeera pleading: "Let Mohammed be the last journalist Israel kills. We don't want any more journalists targeted. My message to the world is to stop the occupation from killing journalists."

His global call went unanswered, and shortly afterwards, Ahmed was killed by the Israeli army.

In a study published on 1 April 2025, Brown University's Costs of War Project concluded that the war on Gaza had killed more journalists since October 2023 than the US Civil War, the First and Second World Wars, the Korean War, the Vietnam War - including the conflicts in Cambodia and Laos - the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s and 2000s, and the post-9/11 war in Afghanistan combined.

Moreover, in its annual round-up published in December 2025, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) found Israel responsible for nearly half of all journalist killings recorded worldwide that year, making occupied Palestine the most dangerous place in the world for journalists.

By the previous August, the organisation had already documented some 220 journalists killed by Israeli forces in the Gaza Strip in less than 23 months.

Why does Israel kill Palestinian journalists? Just as it kills children and other civilians, bombs hospitals and destroys infrastructure, it feels no obligation to offer convincing justifications, because it believes that it is immune from accountability.

The journalists' tent

In November 2023, I was discharged from Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza after receiving treatment for injuries sustained in an Israeli air strike that targeted my home and killed seven members of my family, including my son Abdullah.

I had to leave my hospital bed to make room for another wounded person, given the influx of thousands of casualties.

I had nowhere else to go. Our house was destroyed, my family was displaced, and I still needed time to recover.

A group of journalists welcomed me. They had set up a tent in the hospital courtyard for their work, and they offered to host me there.

They took me in, shared their food with me and gave me a place to sleep. I stayed with them for a month, until we were forced to evacuate when the Israeli military invaded Khan Younis and its tanks advanced towards the hospital.

Looking back, I can count at least four of the journalists I lived with in that tent who were later killed by the Israeli army

About eight journalists slept in that tent at night, and by day it became a busy newsroom frequented by about 20.

Looking back, I can count at least four of the journalists I lived with in that tent who were later killed by the Israeli army: Hassan Islayeh, Mohammed al-Bardawil, Mustafa Thuraya and Mohammed Abu Saada.

Another, Ismail Abu Omar, survived a direct Israeli drone strike but lost a leg.

I do not know what happened to the others. Communication was lost, and news from Gaza became increasingly difficult to follow amid the overwhelming scale of events.

Islayeh, one of Gaza's best-known local journalists, was first targeted by the Israeli military while he was in his tent. He was wounded, but survived.

He was then targeted a second time while lying injured in a bed at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, where he was killed on 13 May 2025.

In its statement on his killing, the Israeli military claimed without evidence that he was a Hamas member, and cited among its justifications his having documented the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.

But documenting those scenes is nothing more than professional work. Islayeh obtained those exclusive shots because he lived near the eastern fence in Khan Younis, which allowed him to arrive quickly and document with his camera.

Any journalist of any nationality near the location at that time would likely have done the same.

Killing the witness

On 10 August 2025, Israel killed six journalists who were sleeping in a tent near al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, among them Al Jazeera correspondent Anas al-Sharif.

Shortly after the strike, the Israeli military posted that Sharif "was the head of a Hamas terrorist cell and advanced rocket attacks on Israeli civilians and IDF troops".

An easy way to deflect criticism after targeting journalists is to claim they were killed by mistake, or that they were not civilians because they were affiliated with Hamas.

Yet the military offered no explanation for the killing of the five other journalists who died in the same attack, despite being fully aware that they were inside the tent with him.

Israel possesses advanced surveillance and intelligence capabilities that enable it to monitor potential targets before carrying out strikes.

As the cases of Sharif and Islayeh show, the Israeli military's most common allegation is that the journalists it targets are affiliated with Hamas.

However, Israel does not define what such affiliation means. The claim is difficult to verify objectively, and many journalists have been killed while clearly engaged in their reporting duties on the ground.

As Muhammad Shehada argued in an analysis for the Israeli independent magazine +972, Israel's record-breaking killing of Palestinian journalists serves a longer-term goal: the destruction of first-person testimony and evidence of its war crimes.

"Journalists in Gaza are often first at the sites of atrocities, mapping out attacks and reaching victims and witnesses," he wrote. "Silencing them eliminates vast troves of incriminating information."

On 11 May 2022, Israeli forces killed the Palestinian journalist Shireen Abu Akleh while she was reporting in the Jenin refugee camp in the occupied West Bank.

She was a Christian Palestinian who did not wear a headscarf, held American citizenship and lived in Jerusalem - a profile that makes any allegation of Hamas affiliation implausible even on Israel's own terms.

She was killed by the same army that has killed Islayeh, Sharif and more than 200 journalists in Gaza. The goal is always the same: to kill the witness who documents the crime.

Follow Middle East Eye's live coverage of Israel's genocide in Gaza

At a lecture, I was asked whether the absence of international journalists in Gaza was a valid explanation for the weakness of media coverage.

I replied that the party categorically preventing foreign journalists from entering Gaza is the Israeli army, and that prohibition is a direct indictment of it, a clear indication of the Israeli war criminals' intention to conceal the truth.

We should nonetheless be careful with the term "international journalists", so that it does not imply that those working inside the Gaza Strip are less competent.

No race or culture entitles a journalist to the title of "international" to the exclusion of others. International journalists come from diverse countries, and Palestinian journalists are international journalists, too.

They are already present in Gaza, direct witnesses to Israel's crimes, and they have documented those crimes in hundreds of thousands of videos, photographs and reports. They work with all the major international outlets and international organisations, and the United Nations rely on their work.

If Israel is going to accuse Gaza's journalists of lacking credibility, why has it not opened the doors for journalists from abroad to come and document the reality for themselves?

The illusion of neutrality

Any attempt to justify the killing of more than 200 journalists is flimsy. Israel has no convincing case against the majority of them, and no affiliation with any faction could justify their murders.

Even if it were established that some Palestinian journalists were affiliated with Palestinian political movements, why should that, in principle, justify their killing?

Any journalist anywhere in the world grows up within a national and cultural context that shapes their identity and life direction, and it is absurd to assume that a journalist can be separated from the context in which they were raised.

The Palestinian people have been struggling against colonialism for a century, and the demand for national rights has formed the consciousness of generations.

It is as unrealistic to strip Palestinian journalists of their natural national affiliation as it would have been to condemn a Dutch journalist for supporting the national resistance against the Nazi invasion in the 1940s.

Israel kills the journalists. Western media kills the truth of genocide in Gaza
Read More »

During media interviews and speeches in the Netherlands, I was asked about neutrality in journalistic work. One journalist expressed surprise that I combine the roles of journalist and activist, and wondered whether the two can work together.

My answer is that neutrality is an illusion. When a journalist witnesses a soldier killing a child, how can they be neutral?

There is no such thing as neutrality, only the objective reporting of facts. Israel's horrific crimes in Gaza require nothing more than their documentation.

When people die of starvation in Gaza, it is impossible to avoid mentioning that Israel is preventing food trucks from reaching civilians. When hundreds of thousands of civilians flee their homes, it is impossible to avoid mentioning the forced displacement orders issued by the Israeli army.

These facts cannot be diluted under the guise of neutrality. Neutrality in this context is siding with the aggressor and participating in the crime.

Another question concerned whether a journalist who is close to events is more likely to be swayed by emotion, while a distant journalist is more objective.

I respond with a counter-question. Is emotional engagement with an event a source of strength or of weakness for a journalist? Is emotional detachment really a prerequisite for good journalism?

Emotional engagement breathes life into journalism, whereas reporting from a distance often presents statistics and figures with little sense of the human experience behind them. Audiences do not follow the news merely to absorb numbers; they look for a living story that speaks to them on a human level.

Consider the difference between a journalist working from an office outside Gaza who writes a report, supported by statistics, about the suffering of people living in tents in the scorching heat, and a journalist living in a tent who writes a story shaped by personal experience.

Which story is more likely to feel alive?

Compare, too, a distant journalist preparing a report on casualty figures with one who has lost a brother or a mother and writes about that loss while still adhering to the professional standards of the craft.

Journalism does not require journalists to be emotionally detached. It requires accuracy and objectivity, qualities that Gaza's journalists have demonstrated with professionalism and distinction.

After all, the best people to tell a story are often those who have lived through it.

Moussawi, who, as head of Hezbollah’s border and resources department, is responsible for many Israeli affairs, said the Lebanese armed movement will continue to fight the occupying troops until they completely depart from his country.

“Is there international pressure that would compel the Israelis to withdraw? So far, there is not, just as there was not in Palestine,” he said.

Hezbollah launched cross-border strikes against Israel the day after the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks, initiating a “support front” to draw resources away from Israel’s war machine as the genocide in Gaza began.

Since then, Israel and Hezbollah have fought two wars: the first of which wiped out much of Hezbollah’s military capabilities and senior leadership, including its longtime secretary-general Hassan Nasrallah.

“We were fulfilling our duty towards the Palestinian resistance. It was therefore no secret that we were providing them with support wherever we could,” Moussawi said.

The second conflict, which Hezbollah launched in March, was sparked by the US-Israeli war on Iran and the killing of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, an important spiritual and political figurehead for the party.

It also, Hezbollah and Israeli media reports suggest, pre-empted a new Israeli offensive on Lebanon following a 15-month period when Israel constantly violated a ceasefire and entrenched itself in occupied territory along the border.

The decision to enter the Iran war and escalate Israeli attacks on Lebanon has been met with incredulity and anger from many Lebanese as well as critics abroad.

At least 4,348 people have been killed in Lebanon since March, and much more Lebanese territory has been occupied since.

Moussawi says blame should be reversed: it is the Israelis, as the occupying force, who are culpable.

“At one point, Israeli propaganda claimed that Fatah was the problem. Now, the problem is said to be Hamas. In the future, the problem will be said to be any Palestinian organisation that seeks to work towards liberating its land,” he said.

The resurrection of Hezbollah
Read More »

“The problem, therefore, is always the occupation, not the organisation resisting that occupation. For example, they now say that Hezbollah is the problem.”

Israel, Moussawi said, would have a problem with any organisation expressing the will of the Lebanese people to liberate their land, “even if it was called the Democratic Party of America”.

Moussawi said the US-backed Israeli attacks on Palestine and Lebanon since October 2023 have attempted to wreak such devastation that “people whose land is occupied feel that resistance is not an option, because it will lead to their destruction”.

“The Palestinian people, for example, tried the path of negotiations through the Palestine Liberation Organisation to the very end, yet did not obtain a Palestinian state,” he added.

“So what can they do? Surrender to the Israeli side? Even surrender is not acceptable to the Israeli side, because what the Israelis want is the extermination of the Palestinian people.”

'Negotiating with Israel has certain requirements'

Since April, the Lebanese state, through the presidency and embassy in Washington, has held direct negotiations with Israel seeking to secure a permanent ceasefire, the withdrawal of Israeli troops and decouple Lebanon from the war on Iran.

Those talks have resulted in a US-backed framework, which seeks to lay out a path towards ending hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah.

It has triggered widespread opposition in Lebanon, raising questions over sovereignty, accountability and provisions that place Lebanese obligations ahead of Israeli commitments.

Hezbollah has denounced the framework as failing to guarantee Israel’s full withdrawal from the six percent of Lebanese territory it continues to occupy and the return of hundreds of thousands of displaced residents to the south.

Lebanon’s Mitri says divisive Israel framework still lacks government approval
Read More »

Moussawi previously served as head of the party’s foreign relations department and an MP, and was heavily involved in negotiations with the Israelis in the 2006 war and over Lebanon’s maritime border with Israel.

He has been highly critical of the way the Lebanese state’s negotiations with Israel have been conducted.

“So far, the Lebanese authorities have not achieved any result,” he told MEE.

As part of the framework, the Lebanese military has been allowed by Israeli troops to deploy in one village in south Lebanon, even though the Israelis never occupied it in the first place.

Talks to secure more villages currently under Israeli occupation have so far been unsuccessful, especially as bombings and skirmishes become more frequent.

“The problem with the negotiations which the president of the republic has now entered into is that he did so without national unity,” said Moussawi.

“In other words, what he is doing does not have the approval of the Lebanese political forces. In Lebanon, such steps must be supported by national consensus.”

Another major issue, Moussawi said, is that “negotiating with Israel has certain requirements, foremost among them being that you enter negotiations holding sources of leverage”.

Moussawi suggested that Aoun may have achieved better results if he had worked in lockstep with Hezbollah, using its armed resistance as a pressure point on the Israelis.

“The resistance, for example, is a source of strength, but he chose to place himself in confrontation with the resistance,” he said.

“How can you achieve liberation when you are at odds with your own people? That is the president's problem.”

'Our way of returning our people to the south is to liberate their land. Liberating the land requires fighting the Israeli occupier and driving it back'

- Nawaf Moussawi

That said, half a million Lebanese - the vast majority from the Shia community that Hezbollah says it represents and protects - have been displaced in this last war.

Hezbollah has pivoted to a tactic that allows its units to cede territory with the aim of harrying Israeli troops that then deploy there. It has proved effective, but also contributed to even more of south Lebanon falling under occupation.

Moussawi insists that armed resistance will return the displaced to their homes - or at least their land after Israel razed strings of villages and towns to the ground.

“Our way of returning our people to the south is to liberate their land. Liberating the land requires fighting the Israeli occupier and driving it back,” he said.

“That is what we did in 2000. This is our path.”

If Aoun had secured an Israeli withdrawal, he would have made himself a hero, Moussawi said. “He has not even been able to stop the destruction within the occupied villages,” he added.

“Despite all the concessions made by the president, the Israelis did not grant him a single gain. Therefore, we have no choice but to resist.”

Confrontations with the army

Also looming over Hezbollah’s relationship with the state is the issue of disarmament.

Days after the party launched six rockets at Israel on 2 March in response to Khamenei’s killing, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam outlawed Hezbollah military activity. The state, Salam insists, must have a monopoly on the use of arms.

There has since been pressure from Israel, Washington and some domestically for the Lebanese military to take a more proactive and confrontational role with Hezbollah and its potential disarmament.

Moussawi believes the framework was designed to create such a scenario, “to shift the problem into Lebanon itself, so that the Lebanese would fight among themselves instead of fighting the Israeli occupier”.

“I do not believe that anyone in Lebanon could take up arms against the resistance to the occupation, because that would mean their own destruction before the destruction of Lebanon,” Moussawi said.

“Does the president of the republic intend to fight the resistance?” he asked.

“I say that even if he were thinking in this way, he could not do it, because the army and security services in Lebanon do not belong to the president. They belong to the Lebanese people, and the Lebanese people will not fight among themselves.”

'Does the president of the republic intend to fight the resistance?'

- Nawaf Moussawi

Another scenario proposed by US President Donald Trump is to have Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who fought Hezbollah for a decade in Syria, use his country’s army to confront the party.

This, Moussawi suggested, “was wishful thinking that cannot become reality”.

The Hezbollah official noted that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a close ally of Sharaa’s, recently said that Turkey’s security begins in Beirut.

“Of course, he was speaking in the context of confronting Israeli expansion,” Moussawi said.

“How, then, could the new Syrian government, which is allied with Turkey, become an instrument for advancing Benjamin Netanyahu's interests and expanding his power in the region?”

Notably, Moussawi opened the possibility of dialogue with Damascus via Ankara.

“We are engaged in genuine and effective dialogue with Turkey, through which new avenues can be opened with the emerging actors in the region.”

After the 2024 war, Hezbollah’s military wing appeared badly degraded. Most of its leadership and commanders had been killed, as well as their deputies, and it seemed unable to go toe to toe with Israel anytime soon, if ever.

However, as MEE revealed in an investigation earlier this month, the party reorganised itself and doubled down on its drone programme, which it staffed with video gamers.

Moussawi acknowledged that Hezbollah had been badly penetrated by Israeli intelligence, “but it is now fighting a generation it does not know”.

This fourth generation of Hezbollah military commanders “were not included on the targeting lists, whether for intelligence or operational purposes”, he noted.

“Therefore, the brothers now operate with greater ease than their brothers who were martyred before them.”

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US vows to 'collapse' Iran with new sanctions as energy prices spike
item.description:
US vows to 'collapse' Iran with new sanctions as energy prices spike

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 08/20/2026 - 19:32
Soaring commodity and shipping prices underscore the risks of inflation as US readies 'economic D-Day'
US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks to members of the press outside the White House on 20 August 2026, in Washington, DC (Alex Wong/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

The US will impose "the toughest sanctions in history” on Iran, Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said on Thursday, vowing to ramp up economic pressure on the Islamic Republic even as the economic toll of the war builds.

"It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade [on Iran], and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history," Bessent told CNBC.

"It is going to work in Iran, and we are going to collapse this regime,” he said, adding that the sanctions will be explained on Monday.

Bessent’s statements come a day after Trump said that he was launching an "economic D-Day" on Iran.

"ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences," Trump said.

The Trump administration’s threats come as it continues to be unable to militarily assert its control over the Strait of Hormuz, with a ceasefire between the two countries all but collapsed.

Energy prices are rising again, posing a problem for the Trump administration as it tries to tame rising borrowing costs.

Brent Oil, the international benchmark, was up two percent on Thursday, trading at $93.41 per barrel. 

The war has also upended the global shipping trade, with the cost of chartering a tanker skyrocketing. BWET, an Exchange Traded Fund (ETF) that allows investors to bet on the shipping rates, has soared 98 percent over the past month.

Asked about rising energy prices, Bessent said, ”We have asymmetric information, and I'm not sure why oil has popped up on this."

Iran has continued attacking vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, while its partner in Yemen, the Houthis, has imposed a maritime blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. The kingdom, which relies on the waterway to export oil, has been forced to pipe crude to the Mediterranean via Egypt.

Sanctions

The US has already imposed debilitating sanctions against Iran. The June ceasefire extension the two sides struck granted Iran a waiver to sell its oil sanctions-free, but the sanctions were reimposed in July. 

Oil supertankers in Gulf are renting for $500,000 per day: Report
Read More »

Iran’s main source of external revenue comes from oil sales by sea. Trump has boasted that the blockade is "extremely effective”.

Iran’s most important economic partner is China, which buys more than 80 percent of its seaborne oil. Experts say that the US would need to impose secondary sanctions on China in order to fully isolate the Islamic Republic.

"We are confident that everyone wants the Strait reopened, and for energy prices to come back down,” Bessent said when asked whether or not the US would impose secondary sanctions on China.

”Keep in mind that the Chinese get 50 percent [of their] energy from inside the Gulf. So it would do them a big service to get with the programme,” he added.

The UAE has also historically served as a key financial hub for Iran.

The UAE said this week that it was halting all trade and financial transactions with Iran.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a phone call this week with UAE national security advisor Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan.

item.description:
Israeli opinion article says Turkey's Nato protection does not apply to troops in Syria

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 08/20/2026 - 19:39
The commentary was published in Israel Hayom, which is owned by the same Israeli mega-donor backing US President Donald Trump
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan walks arm in arm alongside US President Donald Trump at Etimesgut Air Base near Ankara, Turkey, on 7 July 2026 (Mustafa Kamaci/Turkish Presidency Press Office handout via AFP)
Off

An opinion article on Thursday in the right-wing Israeli paper Israel Hayom has suggested that any Turkish troops in Syria would be considered sitting ducks for Israel, because Nato's collective defence pact would not apply outside a member state's borders.

The piece comes two days after Israeli air strikes destroyed parts of a disused air force base in northern Syria, close to the Turkish border, where Israel believed Turkish troops were on the cusp of moving in.

"Before Turkish troops arrive, the target is infrastructure; once they arrive, striking it also risks Turkish casualties, retaliation, American intervention and confrontation with a NATO member. Those costs alter the calculation, not Israel's authority to decide," Shay Gal, head of government relations and strategy firm Line of State, wrote in the Israel Hayom opinion piece.

Israel, he said, "has studied not only how NATO's Article 5 operates, but where it applies. The treaty protects Turkish territory; Turkish troops do not carry that territory with them onto Syrian or occupied Cypriot soil." 

Israel Hayom is published by Miriam Adelson, an Israeli American who is the top donor to Trump, and, by the president's own admission, has considerable sway over his policies towards Israel. 

Israeli officials have made no secret of perceiving Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government as an enemy that wants to weaken it. But under US President Donald Trump, Washington is growing closer to Ankara than ever.

US ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Syria Tom Barrack said Turkey was not warned about the strikes, despite a deconfliction line with Israel in Syria established last year. 

Barrack suggested in an interview with Reuters this week that communication had broken down. 

"This underscores the need for a deconfliction mechanism involving Israel, Syria and Turkey. That ​is something we are actively working on to establish in order to prevent future miscommunication," he said. 

The Israel Hayom article warned that Turkey's close security ties to Damascus are a threat to Israel. 

"Turkey's Syrian project has moved beyond political influence," Gal wrote. "Ankara trains Syrian forces and rebuilds military institutions. In 2025 Turkish military teams examined T4, Palmyra, and Hama as sites for Turkish military depth. Israel subsequently struck those facilities."

Israel, the article says, "acted before Turkish military depth matured" to become an "occupation" such as that of northern Cyprus. 

'Unnecessary escalation'

Barrack defended the Syrian government on Tuesday after Israeli air strikes targeted the Abu al-Duhur military air base, calling it an "unnecessary escalation". 

"The Al-Sharaa government has neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces. It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel," he wrote on X. 

"We are deeply concerned," he added. "[This] does not advance regional stability." 

'Playing with fire': Israel's Syria strike tests Turkey after Mecca defence pact
Read More »

The Syrian government condemned the attack and said eight strikes hit the runway of the defunct air base in the early Tuesday morning hours, local time. 

The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said the strikes followed a visit by a Turkish military delegation to the airfield in recent days "as part of efforts to reactivate it". 

Since former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia in December 2024, Israel has consistently targeted sites along Syria's western border and its north, focusing on degrading the Syrian air force.

It has also sent ground troops into a United Nations-operated buffer zone between the two countries.

The Israeli prime minister’s office said in a statement late on Tuesday that Israel and Syria had agreed to maintain the security status quo, “which Syria was on the verge of breaching by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at an airbase near Aleppo”.

Syrian officials told Middle East Eye that a Turkish technical team had been tasked with repairing the runway and control tower and that there was no military presence at the base.

“The last team tasked with reconstructing the base was there two days beforehand,” one official said.

The officials added that Turkey had been helping the Syrian army build bases across the country, without any specific plans directed at Israel. Ankara, they said, wants to rebuild a robust Syrian military capable of defending the country.

“Turkey doesn’t take over every base,” one official added.

Ankara has, in fact, closed many smaller military outposts in northern Syria and already operates several established bases in the area.
